query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys, toughness retention is governed by a balanced dual‐phase microstructure in which a finely dispersed, coherent precipitate phase (or lamellar structure) interacts with the matrix to activate multiple plasticity mechanisms and blunt stress concentrations; if these precipitates maintain an optimal size and coherence during thermal exposure, toughness is preserved, but if they coarsen or lose interface coherence, the alloy loses toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast equiatomic or near‐equiatomic high‐entropy alloy with a dual‐phase microstructure (e.g., an FCC matrix containing coherent L1_2 or similar nanoprecipitates) that exhibits a favorable combination of strength and ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal treatment (or high-pressure high-temperature processing) designed to tune the precipitate size and interface coherence. For instance, aging at a moderate temperature (e.g., below ~700 °C) for a precise time interval to promote nucleation without significant coarsening.
generation.conditions: The controlled thermal aging should be conducted under an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, within the temperature and time domain where precipitate growth remains limited. Tests should compare samples aged optimally versus those subjected to extended or higher temperature treatments.
generation.structural_mediator: The volume fraction, size, and coherence of the nanoprecipitates (or lamellar colonies) at the matrix interface serve as the mediator; their state determines dislocation mobility and stress distribution during deformation.
generation.mechanism: Coherent nanoprecipitates promote toughness by enabling multiple deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation slip, twinning, and transformation‐induced plasticity) and by reducing local stress concentrations. In contrast, over-aging or thermal exposure that leads to precipitate coarsening or loss of coherence creates localized strain concentrations, making the alloy more prone to crack initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to the optimal thermal treatment will exhibit higher fracture toughness and improved ductility in mechanical tests relative to the as‐cast baseline, while samples that are over-aged (showing precipitate coarsening or loss of interface coherence) will display reduced toughness and earlier crack formation.
generation.baseline: The untreated or as‐cast alloy with its initial dual‐phase microstructure serves as the baseline for assessing toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic hypothesis is expected to hold for high‐entropy alloys that derive their toughness from a coherent dual‐phase microstructure (e.g., FCC matrix with L1_2-type precipitates) within a temperature regime up to approximately 700 °C and under controlled inert atmospheres; it may not apply to alloys that form brittle intermetallic compounds or that undergo significant oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature and time thresholds that lead to precipitate coarsening, as well as the influence of different secondary alloying elements on phase stability and interface coherence, remain uncertain and would require detailed in situ characterization and mechanical testing for quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of the same high‐entropy alloy with the baseline dual‐phase microstructure. Subject one set to an optimized thermal aging treatment (e.g., moderate temperature for a precise time to maintain precipitate coherence) and another set to over-aging conditions (e.g., higher temperature or longer duration to induce precipitate coarsening). Perform standardized fracture toughness and tensile tests, and use in situ electron microscopy to quantify precipitate size, distribution, and interface coherence.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC) and tensile ductility measurements
Precipitate size and coherence via TEM or STEM
Dislocation activity and deformation mechanisms via in situ microscopy
Comparison of crack initiation and propagation behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized thermal treatment does not result in a statistically significant improvement in toughness (e.g., higher K_IC and ductility) relative to the baseline, or if over-aging does not lead to measurable precipitate coarsening, loss of interface coherence, and reduced toughness, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.
